summary: Defines a generic echo request and reply format that lets the node starting IOAM discover the IOAM capabilities of the transit and decapsulating nodes in an IOAM domain. It is meant to be used over data planes such as IPv6, MPLS, SFC, and BIER.

plainLanguage.summary: Before a team starts a game, the captain asks each player what they can do. This is that roll call for routers in a measurement system.

questions: how does an ioam encapsulating node discover capabilities
subtitle: A generic echo request and reply format that lets an IOAM edge node ask each node on a path which IOAM features it has turned on.

tldr.problem: When no central controller manages every IOAM device, the node that adds IOAM headers has no easy way to learn which IOAM capabilities the other nodes on the path have enabled. NETCONF/YANG and IGP both have limits here.
tldr.mechanism: It defines a Capabilities Query Container for echo requests and a Capabilities Response Container with six object types for echo replies, probed hop by hop with increasing TTL.
tldr.outcome: The encapsulating node can build the correct IOAM header from what it discovers. The RFC defines only the generic formats; container and object headers and type registries are left to later documents per data plane.

today: RFC 9359 is a Proposed Standard (April 2023) and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines only the generic formats, so each echo protocol needs its own document to carry them.

sections.title: The Discovery Problem in IOAM
sections.content:
In situ OAM (IOAM) records operations and telemetry data inside the packet as it crosses a network domain, called an IOAM-Domain. The node that adds the IOAM header is the IOAM encapsulating node, the node that removes it is the IOAM decapsulating node, and nodes in between that read or write IOAM data are IOAM transit nodes.

If a control entity manages every IOAM device, it can provision the headers directly. Without one, the encapsulating node must discover what the transit and decapsulating nodes have enabled, so it can choose the right IOAM option types and lengths.

The RFC names the limits of the alternatives. With NETCONF/YANG, each encapsulating node needs a NETCONF client, each other node a server, and a connection to each, so complexity and scalability are issues. With an IGP, coverage may not match the IOAM-Domain, for example when a host is an edge node, and capabilities controlled by local policy depending on the encapsulating node's identity are hard to reflect.
sections.plainLanguage: The captain needs to know what each player can do before choosing the game plan. Asking each one directly is simpler than the other ways.

sections.title: Scope and Fate Sharing
sections.content:
The RFC specifies formats and objects for extending echo request/reply mechanisms in IPv6 (including SRv6), MPLS (including SR-MPLS), SFC and BIER environments. It lists the related documents, such as RFC 4620 and RFC 8029. The actual instantiation in each protocol is expected to be a separate RFC from the working group that maintains that echo protocol together with the IPPM working group.

For IPv6, the echo mechanism meant here is the IPv6 Node Information Query/Reply of RFC 4620, not the ICMPv6 Echo Request/Reply.

The echo request must share fate with IOAM data packets: it has to traverse the same path, for instance by using the same explicit path or by populating the same values in any ECMP-affecting fields.
sections.plainLanguage: The roll-call question has to travel down the same road the game traffic will use, or the answers would be about the wrong road.

sections.title: The Query and Response Containers
sections.content:
An echo request carries an IOAM Capabilities Query Container: a container header plus a list of IOAM Namespace-IDs. The list MUST have at least one entry, and if the Default-Namespace-ID 0x0000 is present it MUST be first; later occurrences of 0x0000 MUST be disregarded. The sender asks only for enabled capabilities matching one of those Namespace-IDs. If the receiver has nothing to report, it ignores the container.

An echo reply from an IOAM transit or decapsulating node carries an IOAM Capabilities Response Container, with a container header and a list of capabilities objects. The list MUST be included unless the sender hits an error such as no matching Namespace-ID. The same object type MAY appear more than once only with different Namespace-IDs.

The container and object headers are deliberately not defined: their length, structure and definition depend on the deployment environment. Containers and object payloads MUST fall on a 4-octet boundary.
sections.plainLanguage: The question lists the 'teams' the captain cares about. The answer lists what each player can do for those teams.

sections.title: The Six Capability Objects
sections.content:
Based on RFC 9197 and RFC 9326, six object types are defined. Each reports an enabled function and echoes a Namespace-ID that MUST be one from the query.

  • Pre-allocated Tracing and Incremental Tracing (transit nodes): IOAM-Trace-Type, a W flag for short or wide Ingress_if_id, Namespace-ID, a 16-bit Ingress_MTU and Ingress_if_id (16 bits short, 32 bits wide).
  • Proof of Transit (transit nodes): Namespace-ID, IOAM-POT-Type and a 2-bit SoP field. 0b00 means 64-bit PktID and 64-bit Cumulative data; the other values are reserved.
  • Edge-to-Edge (decapsulating nodes): Namespace-ID, IOAM-E2E-Type and a 2-bit TSF timestamp format field: 0b00 PTP truncated, 0b01 NTP 64-bit, 0b10 POSIX-based, 0b11 reserved.
  • DEX (transit nodes): IOAM-Trace-Type and Namespace-ID, showing direct exporting is enabled.
  • End-of-Domain (decapsulating nodes): just a Namespace-ID, to mark the end of the domain.

Reserved fields MUST be zeroed on transmission and ignored on receipt. An IOAM decapsulating node MUST include the End-of-Domain object unless the Edge-to-Edge object is present, and when edge-to-edge is enabled, sending only the Edge-to-Edge object is RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of player answers with a little form. One form says how they track the ball, one proves they were on the field, one says how they keep time, and one says 'I am the last player'.

sections.title: The Operational Guide
sections.content:
Once triggered, the IOAM encapsulating node sends echo requests with the query container. It starts with TTL equal to 1 to reach the closest node, then TTL 2 for the next, increasing the TTL by 1 each time until it receives a reply from the IOAM decapsulating node, identified by the Edge-to-Edge or End-of-Domain object. That way every node on the path is reached one by one.

If the encapsulating node already knows all the transit and decapsulating nodes, it can send an echo request to each directly, without TTL expiration. Triggering is out of scope; the RFC lists the administrator, a network management system, a controller or data traffic as possible triggers.

A node unaware of IOAM ignores the query container. The mechanism covers all IOAM option types, including DEX, where it reveals which nodes support direct exporting and which trace data types they can export.
sections.plainLanguage: The captain asks the first player, then the second, then the third, moving down the line until the last player answers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
To limit denial-of-service attacks, rate-limiting of incoming echo requests and replies is RECOMMENDED. Implementations MUST provide a way to check the source address of echo requests against an access list. Deployments MUST use border filtering to drop inbound echo requests with an IOAM Capabilities Container Header from outside the domain, and outbound requests or replies with IOAM Capabilities Headers leaving it.

The discovery feature MUST be configurable on or off and MUST be disabled by default. Integrity and confidentiality can be provided by the underlying transport, for example the IP Authentication Header or ESP in IPv6, since capability information may be considered confidential.
sections.plainLanguage: Strangers should not be able to ask the players what they can do, so the roll call is turned off unless you switch it on, and only trusted askers are answered.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content: IANA created a registry named "In Situ OAM (IOAM) Capabilities" with two subregistries. The IOAM SoP Capability registry starts with 0b00 (64-bit PktID and 64-bit Cumulative data) and leaves 0b01 to 0b11 for IETF Review. The IOAM TSF Capability registry starts with 0b00, 0b01 and 0b10 and leaves 0b11 for IETF Review. Registries for container and object types are left to the subsequent documents for each echo protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Two official lists were started, one for proof sizes and one for clock styles, with room to add more later.
